take: Hormuz remains the dominant risk after Iran stated the strait will stay closed until US conditions are met, with vessel traffic collapsing to just six commodity ships on Monday, a development that keeps a hefty geopolitical premium in crude and threatens to reprice product tanker tonne-mile demand. The surprise 9.072 million barrel US crude build reported by the API against a 500,000 barrel expected draw complicates the bullish narrative, though it may reflect disrupted flows seeking alternative discharge rather than weak physical demand. China's second-quarter crude import decline, driven by higher prices from the Hormuz disruption, reinforces the demand-side caution that is capping outright rallies. The Panama Canal's fourth and fifth draft adjustment this year tightens neopanamax transits, adding friction to dry bulk and container schedules and supporting freight rates at a time when Star Bulk's withdrawal from the Genco deal signals consolidation risk in the bulker space. Watch for official EIA inventory data tomorrow to confirm the API build, and any fresh headlines on US-Iran negotiations that could trigger a sharp de-escalation in the crude complex.
